answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I've been at Halstead Systems for about a year, working mostly on our procurement module, which is still built in Java. The transaction-boundary decisions there were made well before I joined, by a senior engineer who owns that part of the codebase -- I know roughly where the boundary sits, around the purchase-order approval step, but I couldn't tell you the reasoning behind it beyond what's in the design doc, since that wasn't my call.
answers.says: Has no experience making transaction boundary design decisions themselves. The answer stops at ‘the team decided’ or ‘a senior engineer designed it,’ and even when asked what part they were responsible for or what they considered, they cannot explain concretely. They claim Java experience, but the answer shows the design decisions were left to others.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: JVM and Kubernetes operations on the Java side are owned by our platform team, not by me. I've watched them work through a slow-query issue once, sitting in on the call, but I wasn't the one running the diagnosis or making the change -- my part there was answering a question about which endpoint the customer had reported as slow.
answers.says: Explains that JVM and Kubernetes operations were handled by other team members or SRE, so they only wrote code and were never directly involved in operational problems. Even when asked about their involvement in triage or measurement, they cannot describe concretely what logs they looked at or what action they took.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: At Halstead, the general approach to avoiding duplicate processing is to use an idempotency key on requests that could otherwise be retried, and if a mismatch ever comes up, the principle is to correct it with a new entry rather than editing what's already there, so there's a clear record of what happened. I understand why that matters for anything involving customer billing. I haven't personally been the one to design or debug that kind of system, though -- at my company, that's generally handled by the billing team, not by anyone on the ERP product side.
answers.says: Has no real example of duplication or a mismatch they personally handled; the answer stops at ‘the team handled it,’ and even when asked about their own role, they cannot explain concretely. Or, they cannot describe any experience handling a consistency mismatch at all.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: The closest incident I've owned myself involved the Rust import service -- it was rejecting a batch of otherwise-valid rows because of an encoding edge case, non-UTF8 bytes in a legacy customer export, that I hadn't accounted for. I found it because the customer's support ticket came to me directly, since I own that service; I had a fix -- falling back to a lossy conversion with a warning flag rather than a hard failure -- deployed within about a day, and added a test case for that encoding specifically afterward.
answers.says: Describes an incident in a system they operated, with a timeline and numbers (time from detection, time to recovery, number of affected cases). Explains, in their own words, what they looked at to triage the cause and the recovery decisions (including who they told and when), and can describe the postmortem's preventive measures and whether they actually worked afterward. If their own mistake caused it, they can describe, matter-of-factly, how they shared that without hiding it.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I actually do have production Rust experience, which is a bit unusual for someone one year in. Alongside the Java procurement module, I built and now maintain a Rust service that handles bulk CSV import for customer product catalogs -- some of our larger ERP customers upload catalogs with over 200,000 line items, and the old Java importer was taking upwards of 25 minutes and occasionally timing out. I picked Rust specifically because the bottleneck was CPU-bound parsing and validation, not I/O, and I wanted predictable memory use without GC pauses on a job that size. The rewrite brought import time down to under 90 seconds for the same 200,000-line file.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: The clearest example is from the import service: early on I had a function that needed to process file chunks across multiple threads, and I kept hitting Send-trait errors because I was trying to share a non-thread-safe buffer across threads without realizing it. I ended up wrapping the shared state in an Arc-Mutex at first, which worked but was slower than I wanted under contention, and eventually restructured the code so each thread owned its own buffer and results were merged at the end instead of sharing a single one -- no locking needed at all. That restructuring is what's still running in production.
answers.says: Names concretely what failed to compile in their own code (e.g., a borrow conflict, a lifetime annotation, a Send/Sync constraint, a tokio runtime boundary), how they fixed it, and how they came to understand the fix, in their own words. If it was production work, which part of production it was comes out concretely; if personal, what they built comes out concretely.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: For the CSV importer, I kept the boundary narrow: the Rust service only does parsing, validation, and producing a normalized batch of records -- it doesn't own any persistence or talk to the database directly. It receives a file reference over an internal HTTP call from the Java side and returns a validated batch, which the Java side then writes to Postgres inside its own transaction. I measured parse-and-validate time and peak memory before and after: the old Java parser peaked around 4GB of heap on the largest files, and the Rust service peaks under 300MB for the same input. Keeping persistence in Java meant I didn't have to solve transactional consistency across two languages at all.
answers.says: Concretely describes how to choose a migration target (measuring hot paths, starting with lower-risk parts), how to place the boundary (the shape of the interface, how to keep data consistent, coexisting with Java), and what metrics to watch before and after migration (latency, memory, correctness reconciliation), together with their own grounds for those decisions. If they've carved out a boundary before, they include the numbers, failures, and how they built agreement with the team. Fits our ‘decide the boundary before you rewrite’ approach, and can also describe how they resisted the temptation to do a full rewrite.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: I haven't led a data-recovery effort in the Java procurement module myself. There was one case where some purchase orders ended up in an inconsistent approval state after a bug, and a senior engineer investigated and wrote the fix -- I helped by running a query he gave me to count how many orders were affected, but the actual scoping and fix were his.
answers.says: Explains that restoring consistency was handled by a DBA or a different team, so they weren't involved. Even when asked about scoping or verification, they cannot describe concretely what they looked at or what they did.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: I haven't had a real emergency come up yet in my year here, so I don't have a live example of being tempted to skip review. What I can say is that on the Rust import service, even for what felt like a low-risk change, I've stuck to getting a review every time, partly because I'm still new enough that I don't trust my own judgment on that service to be the only check.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about a concrete incident where the numbers didn't match in settlement or reconciliation. What was off, by how much, how did you notice, what was the cause, and how did you correct it? Please also cover how you handled data after it was finalized.
answers.answer: I understand the general idea of why reconciliation numbers might not match -- timing differences, a refund landing after a period closes, that kind of thing -- and that you correct it with a new entry instead of overwriting history. I haven't personally chased a mismatch like that, though; billing and reconciliation are handled by a different team at Halstead, and I've only seen it discussed in cross-team meetings, not worked it myself.
answers.says: Describes that a mismatch occurred, but someone else did the investigation, and they cannot explain their own role concretely even when asked. The cause and the fix end at 'it was handled.'

answers.text: I'd like to check something from your earlier answers where you used the phrase 'as a team.' Within that, which parts did you personally decide and do yourself? Please answer the same question again, using a different piece of experience.
answers.answer: In the Rust import service I described, that one was mine end to end -- I designed it, built it, and I'm the one who owns it now. On the Java procurement side, my role is much smaller: I've been assigned self-contained tickets, like adding a new field to the approval form, and the actual system design there belongs to someone more senior. I think it's important to be clear about that difference rather than let the Rust work make the Java side sound bigger than it is.
answers.says: Names a concrete example from their earlier answers, and clearly separates the points they decided alone (a design choice, incident triage, deciding a migration boundary, etc.) from the points left to the team. Can explain, in their own words, the grounds for the decision and the part they did hands-on, and can do the same for a different piece of experience. Comes with numbers and time frames, so 'as a team' is described as an actual division of labor rather than a convenient phrase.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you improved latency or throughput in a production Java service based on measurement. Give me the before-and-after numbers, and if you tried something that didn't work, tell me that too.
answers.answer: No performance change I've driven myself on the Java side. I did once profile a slow endpoint alongside a senior engineer, mostly watching and asking questions about what the flame graph was showing, but the decision about what to change was his, not mine.
answers.says: The improvement was done by the team or other members; they were not directly involved in either the measurement or the change. Cannot describe concretely what they looked at to make the call, even when asked.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
